title: Precision Machining: traditional plantwide overhead vs activity-based costing and product cost distortion
participant_role: Senior cost accountant at Precision Machining reviewing how overhead is assigned to products
judge_role: Chief operating officer (COO) of Precision Machining, puzzled by lost Standard Valve bids and shrinking margins

difficulty.rationale: Activity-based costing vs plantwide rate and cost distortion.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of senior cost accountant for PRECISION MACHINING, a manufacturer of high-precision metal valves for aerospace and medical customers. The chief operating officer (judge) has asked you to review how the company assigns manufacturing overhead to its products.

Precision Machining makes two products. The Standard Valve is a high-volume product: 9,000 units a year, sold at $60 each. The Custom Aerospace Valve is a low-volume, complex product: 1,000 units a year, sold at $70 each. Every valve of either type uses $25 of direct materials and one direct labor hour at $20 per hour.

Total manufacturing overhead is $100,000 a year. The company currently assigns all overhead to products with a single plantwide rate based on direct labor hours. Total direct labor hours are 10,000 (9,000 for Standard Valves and 1,000 for Custom Valves).

The accounting team has studied the overhead and found that it comes from two activities. Machine setups cost $60,000 a year for 100 setups (30 for Standard Valves and 70 for Custom Valves). Quality inspections cost $40,000 a year for 200 inspections (80 for Standard Valves and 120 for Custom Valves).

The COO (judge) is puzzled. Precision keeps losing bids for Standard Valves to lower-priced competitors, yet it wins almost every Custom Valve bid, and overall profit margins keep shrinking.

[Precision Machining product and overhead data: see exhibits]

You must:
- Calculate the unit product cost of each valve under the current plantwide overhead system and under activity-based costing (ABC)
- Quantify how much each product is overcosted or undercosted under the current system
- Explain why the current system distorts product costs
- Recommend pricing and operational changes based on your findings

You will present the information to the COO (judge) in a role-play to take place in the COO's office. The COO (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the COO's (judge's) questions, the COO (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: Can we use these activity-based costs in our audited external financial statements, or only for internal decisions?
If our custom customers refuse to accept a price increase from $70 to $130, what operational actions should we take?

solution.overview: A strong answer computes a $55 unit cost for both valves under the plantwide rate, then uses activity rates of $600 per setup and $200 per inspection to show ABC unit costs of $48.78 (Standard) and $111 (Custom). The presenter shows $56,000 of overhead shifted from Custom to Standard, explains that direct labor hours do not drive setups or inspections, and recommends lowering Standard prices, raising Custom prices above $111 and cutting setups.

answer: Plantwide rate: 100,000 / 10,000 DLH = $10 per DLH, so both valves cost 25 + 20 + 10 = $55
Activity rates: 60,000 / 100 = $600 per setup; 40,000 / 200 = $200 per inspection
Check: 34,000 + 66,000 = $100,000, all overhead assigned
Standard Valve is overcosted by 55 minus 48.78 = $6.22 per unit ($56,000 in total)
Custom Valve is undercosted by 111 minus 55 = $56 per unit ($56,000 in total)
Standard Valves are subsidizing Custom Valves by $56,000 a year
At $70, each Custom Valve loses 70 minus 111 = $41 (a $41,000 loss a year); Standard earns $11.22 per unit, not $5

by_task.task: Why the plantwide system distorts costs
answer: Direct labor hours are a volume-based driver; setups and inspections are driven by batches and complexity
Custom Valves are only 10% of labor hours but cause 70% of setups and 60% of inspections
Spreading overhead by labor hours pushes Custom costs onto the high-volume Standard Valve
ABC links each cost pool to the activity that causes it, so product costs reflect resource use
Lower the Standard Valve price below $60 to win bids; it still earns a profit above its $48.78 cost
Raise the Custom Valve price above its $111 cost (for example, the $130 the COO is considering)
Reduce setups: larger batches, minimum order sizes, standardized parts
Charge a separate setup or engineering fee on small custom orders
Keep using ABC data for bidding and review the cost pools every year

calculations.label: ABC unit cost, Custom Aerospace Valve
Cost distortion and profit at current prices
steps: Standard: overhead assigned 90,000 (traditional) vs 34,000 (ABC), overcosted $56,000 ($6.22 per unit)
Custom: overhead assigned 10,000 (traditional) vs 66,000 (ABC), undercosted $56,000 ($56 per unit)
Standard profit per unit: 60 minus 48.78 = $11.22 (traditional showed $5)
Custom profit per unit: 70 minus 111 = $41 loss (traditional showed $15 profit)
Total gross profit is $60,000 either way: 101,000 minus 41,000 (ABC) = 45,000 + 15,000 (traditional)
calculations.result: $56,000 cross-subsidy from Standard to Custom; Custom loses $41 per unit

judge_question_answers.question: Can we use these activity-based costs in our audited external financial statements, or only for internal decisions?
answer: Yes, as long as it follows absorption costing: inventory must include all manufacturing costs and only manufacturing costs
Setups and inspections are both manufacturing overhead, so our ABC product costs could value inventory under U.S. GAAP
If we extend ABC to selling or administrative costs for pricing, those costs must still be expensed as period costs in the external statements
Many companies use ABC mainly for internal decisions because it costs more to maintain

judge_question_answers.question: If our custom customers refuse to accept a price increase from $70 to $130, what operational actions should we take?
answer: Cut the number of setups: larger production runs, minimum order quantities, fewer design variations
Standardize components and redesign valves for easier manufacturing to reduce setup and inspection time
Add a setup fee to small custom orders so the cost follows the customer who causes it
Drop custom orders whose price does not cover their variable and activity costs

key_concepts.definition: Indirect production costs, such as setups and inspections, that cannot be traced directly to one unit and must be allocated.
One overhead rate for the whole factory. Rate = total overhead / total allocation base (for example, direct labor hours).
A costing system that groups overhead into activity cost pools and assigns it to products based on how much of each activity they use.
A group of overhead costs caused by one activity, such as machine setups or quality inspections.
The factor that causes an activity's cost, such as the number of setups or inspections.
Cost per unit of a driver. Activity rate = cost pool total / total driver quantity.
Direct materials plus direct labor. Prime cost = DM + DL ($45 per valve here).
When one product is assigned too much overhead and another too little, so one product appears less profitable and the other more profitable than it really is.
A product is overcosted when its reported cost is higher than the resources it uses, and undercosted when its reported cost is lower.
The method required for external reporting: product cost includes direct materials, direct labor and all manufacturing overhead, but no selling or administrative costs.

notes: ICDC level because students must build ABC from pool totals and driver counts, then turn the numbers into pricing and operational advice. Watch for students who divide Standard overhead by the number of setups instead of by units, or who recommend dropping Custom Valves without first trying to reprice or cut setups.

criteria.exceeds: Contrasts the single plantwide rate based on direct labor hours with activity-based costing, explains that labor hours are a volume-based driver while setups and inspections are driven by batches and complexity, and shows that Custom Valves use only 10% of labor hours but cause 70% of setups and 60% of inspections.
criteria.meets: Explains that the plantwide rate spreads overhead by direct labor hours, which pushes Custom Valve costs onto the Standard Valve, while ABC links each cost pool to the activity that causes it.
criteria.below: Describes the two systems in general terms but cannot explain why labor hours distort costs here, or says ABC simply gives a different answer without saying why.
criteria.little: Does not describe either costing system, or claims the current plantwide rate is accurate.

criteria.exceeds: Calculates the $10 per labor hour plantwide rate and $55 unit cost, activity rates of $600 per setup and $200 per inspection, ABC unit costs of $48.78 (Standard) and $111 (Custom), and checks that $34,000 plus $66,000 equals the full $100,000 of overhead.
criteria.meets: Calculates the $55 plantwide unit cost for both valves and ABC unit costs of $48.78 for the Standard Valve and $111 for the Custom Valve.
criteria.below: Gets the activity rates right but makes an allocation error, for example dividing Standard overhead by the number of setups instead of by 9,000 units, or finds only one ABC unit cost.
criteria.little: Does not calculate ABC costs, or the numbers are unrelated to the exhibits.

items.label: Explain the nature of managerial accounting

criteria.exceeds: Explains that managerial accounting produces cost information for internal decisions such as bidding and pricing, shows that Standard really earns $11.22 per unit (not $5) while Custom loses $41 per unit (not a $15 profit), and notes total gross profit stays $60,000 under either system, so ABC changes decisions, not total profit.
criteria.meets: Explains that ABC cost data helps managers set prices and win bids, and that it shows the Custom Valve loses $41 per unit at its $70 price.
criteria.below: Mentions that the numbers help management but does not connect them to the lost Standard bids or the Custom Valve pricing decision.
criteria.little: Does not explain how cost information supports management decisions.

items.label: Describe types of costs used in managerial accounting

criteria.exceeds: Identifies direct materials ($25) and direct labor ($20) as traceable direct costs (a $45 prime cost), setups and inspections as indirect manufacturing overhead that must be allocated, and quantifies that the Standard Valve is overcosted by $6.22 per unit and the Custom Valve undercosted by $56 per unit ($56,000 each in total).
criteria.meets: Separates direct costs from manufacturing overhead and states that the Standard Valve is overcosted and the Custom Valve undercosted by $56,000 in total.
criteria.below: Names cost types loosely or gets the direction or size of the overcosting and undercosting partly wrong.
criteria.little: Does not describe any cost types or cannot say which product is overcosted.

criteria.exceeds: Restates the COO's three concerns (lost Standard bids, easy Custom wins, shrinking margins), explains how the $56,000 cross-subsidy causes each one, and answers follow-up questions directly, including the $70 to $130 price question.
criteria.meets: Responds to the COO's specific concerns about lost Standard Valve bids and shrinking margins and answers the judge's questions on topic.
criteria.below: Delivers a prepared presentation that only partly addresses the COO's concerns, or misunderstands a question before answering.
criteria.little: Ignores the COO's concerns and questions, or answers questions that were not asked.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Links the choice of cost driver to distorted unit costs, then to overpricing Standard Valves and underpricing Custom Valves, and finally to lost bids and shrinking margins.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the driver data to the conclusion that Standard Valves subsidize Custom Valves by $56,000.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or misses how the cost distortion affects bidding.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Recommends lowering the Standard price below $60 while staying above $48.78, raising the Custom price above $111 (such as $130), cutting setups through larger batches and minimum order sizes, adding setup fees, and reviewing cost pools every year.
criteria.meets: Recommends lowering Standard Valve prices and raising Custom Valve prices above their $111 ABC cost.
criteria.below: Gives a partly correct recommendation, for example dropping Custom Valves without first trying to reprice or cut setups.
criteria.little: Makes no recommendation, or suggests keeping current prices.

criteria.exceeds: Explains ABC and cross-subsidy in plain language the COO can follow, in a logical order from rates to unit costs to pricing, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the two costing systems, calculations and recommendations clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps in the calculations.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a side by side comparison ($55 against $48.78 and $111) or a simple visual that makes the distortion obvious, and adds practical ideas such as standardized parts or a setup fee on small custom orders.
criteria.meets: Organizes the plantwide and ABC results in a way that makes the difference easy to see.
criteria.below: Presents the numbers with little effort to make them engaging or easy to compare.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: ABC costs can value inventory under U.S. GAAP because setups and inspections are manufacturing overhead (absorption costing), while selling and administrative costs stay period costs; and if customers refuse $130, cut setups, standardize parts, add setup fees and drop orders that do not cover their costs.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that ABC can be used externally if it includes only manufacturing costs and that reducing setups is the key operational fix.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers such as saying ABC is never allowed externally.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or gives incorrect answers.

key_points: Plantwide rate = $100,000 / 10,000 labor hours = $10 per hour, so both valves cost $55
Activity rates: $600 per setup and $200 per inspection
ABC unit costs: Standard Valve $48.78 ($34,000 overhead), Custom Valve $111 ($66,000 overhead)
Standard is overcosted by $6.22 per unit and Custom undercosted by $56 per unit, a $56,000 cross-subsidy
At current prices Standard earns $11.22 per unit while Custom loses $41 per unit
Labor hours are a volume-based driver; Custom Valves use 10% of labor hours but cause 70% of setups and 60% of inspections
Recommend pricing Standard below $60 (above $48.78), pricing Custom above $111, and cutting the number of setups
ABC can value inventory for external statements if it includes only manufacturing costs (absorption costing)
